study_identification.title: Charting brain growth and aging at high spatial precision

study_characteristics.study_objective: To assemble a large neuroimaging reference cohort from 82 sites (N=58,836; ages 2-100) and use normative modeling to characterize lifespan trajectories of cortical thickness and subcortical volume at high spatial resolution, and to showcase the clinical value by applying the models to a transdiagnostic psychiatric sample (N=1985).

dataset_name.answer: Multi-site aggregated dataset (UK Biobank; ABCD; HCP Young Adult; HCP Aging; HCP Development; HCP Early Psychosis; ABIDE; ADHD200; CAMCAN; CMI-HBN; IXI; NKI-RS; Oasis; OpenNeuro; PNC; SRPBS; and 60+ other sites)

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FreeSurfer v6.0; Destrieux parcellation (148 cortical thickness regions and 40 subcortical volumes)

quality_checking_detail.answer: Multi-pronged approach: (1) Manual quality checking (mQC) performed on subset (N=24,354) using Papaya viewer with pass/fail/flag rating of T1w and FreeSurfer brain.finalsurfs overlay; ABCD consortium QC (fsqc_qc variable) included in mQC subset. (2) Automated QC for full sample using FreeSurfer Euler Characteristic (EC), with conservative threshold removing samples in tail of distribution (EC scaled and centered across sites).

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Site variation modeled using fixed effects for site in the normative model (age, sex, and site as covariates). Fixed effects approach shown to provide relatively good performance in prior work, though random effects may provide additional flexibility at higher computational cost. Transfer learning approach provided for adapting models to new sites not in training set by adjusting mean and variance in latent Gaussian space.

modeling_method.answer: BLR with likelihood warping (warped Bayesian Linear Regression)

response_variable.answer: Cortical thickness (148 Destrieux parcellation regions); Subcortical volumes (40 regions)

predictor_effects.answer: Age: fixed effect modeled with B-spline basis expansion (cubic spline with 5 evenly spaced knots) for non-linear effects; Sex: fixed effect; Site: fixed effect. Likelihood warping (sinarcsinh warping function equivalent to SHASH distribution) used to model non-Gaussian effects.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study explicitly addresses multiple nuisance structures: (1) Site/scanner effects are modeled as fixed effects in the normative model; (2) Non-Gaussian distributions are handled via likelihood warping (sinarcsinh function); (3) Non-linear age effects are modeled using B-spline basis expansion with 5 knots; (4) Quality control procedures address image quality issues (Euler Characteristic for automated QC, manual QC for subset); (5) Sex effects are modeled as fixed effects. The paper also discusses model transfer procedures to handle mean/variance shifts when applying to new sites.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: We employed a warped Bayesian linear regression model to accurately model non-linear and non-Gaussian effects (Fraza et al., 2021), whilst accounting for scanner effects (Bayer et al., 2021; Kia et al., 2021). [...] Site variation was modeled using fixed effects, which we have shown in prior work provides relatively good performance (Kia et al., 2021), although random effects for site may provide additional flexibility at higher computational cost. [...] A likelihood warping approach (Rios and Tobar, 2019; Snelson et al., 2003) was used to model non-Gaussian effects. This involves applying a bijective non-linear warping function to the non-Gaussian response variables to map them to a Gaussian latent space where inference can be performed in closed form. We employed a 'sinarcsinsh' warping function, which is equivalent to the SHASH distribution commonly used in the generalized additive modeling literature (Jones and Pewsey, 2009) [...] Given a new set of data (e.g., sites not present in the training set), this is done by first applying the warp parameters estimating on the training data to the new data set, adjusting the mean and variance in the latent Gaussian space, then (if necessary) warping the adjusted data back to the original space
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Page 6, lines 118-121; Materials and methods section, lines 169-178, 180-183

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study uses a held-out test set strategy where the data is split 50/50 into training and test sets, stratified by site. Although both sets come from the same 82 sites (same domain), they represent different individuals, making them independent at the subject level but non-independent at the site/domain level. Evaluation metrics (explained variance, MSLL, skewness, kurtosis) are reported on multiple test sets including the full test set (N=29,418) and manually quality-checked test set (N=12,177). Additionally, 10 random resamplings of the test set were performed to assess stability.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: We split the available data into training and test sets, stratifying by site (Table 1, Supplementary files 1 and 2). [...] Equal sized training and testing data sets (split half) were created using scikit-learn's train_test_split function, stratifying on the site variable. It is important to stratify based on site, not only study (Bethlehem et al., 2021), as many of the public studies (i.e., ABCD) include several sites, thus modeling study does not adequately address MRI scanner confounds. To test stability of the model performance, the full test set was randomly resampled 10 times and evaluation metrics were re-calculated on each split of the full test set (Figure 3-figure supplement 2).
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.location: Results section, lines 84-85; Materials and methods section, lines 155-156; Table 1

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: While the study validates on held-out test subjects from the same 82 sites (which could be considered same-domain validation), true independent same-domain validation would require completely separate cohorts from the same data sources. The manual QC subset (N=24,354) provides some level of independent validation as it uses different quality control procedures, but it's drawn from the same overall sample. The study does not report validation on entirely separate cohorts from the same datasets (e.g., different waves of UK Biobank or ABCD that were collected later).
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: We validate our models with several careful procedures: first, we report out of sample metrics; second, we perform a supplementary analysis on a subset of participants for whom input data had undergone manual quality checking by an expert rater (Table 1 - mQC). [...] We also estimated separate models for males and females, which indicate that sex effects are adequately modeled using a global offset.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study explicitly validates the models on a transfer dataset consisting of 6 sites (N=546) from OpenNeuro that were NOT included in the original training set. This represents true different-domain validation. The transfer procedure involves applying warp parameters from training data, adjusting mean and variance in latent Gaussian space, and the results are reported in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 3. Additionally, the models are applied to clinical cohorts (N=1,985) from 24 sites as another form of different-domain validation.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: To show generalizability of the models to new data not included in training, we leveraged data from OpenNeuro.org (Markiewicz et al., 2021) to create a transfer data set (six sites, N=546, Supplementary file 3). This data are provided along with the code for transferring to walk users through how to apply these models to their own data. [...] Given a new set of data (e.g., sites not present in the training set), this is done by first applying the warp parameters estimating on the training data to the new data set, adjusting the mean and variance in the latent Gaussian space, then (if necessary) warping the adjusted data back to the original space [...] We leveraged data from OpenNeuro.org (Markiewicz et al., 2021) to create a transfer data set (six sites, N=546, Supplementary file 3). These results are reported in Figure 3 (transfer) and Supplementary file 3.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Materials and methods section, lines 155-157, 180-185; Supplementary file 3; Figure 3

clinical_dataset.answer: Transdiagnostic psychiatric sample from 24 sites (subset of full dataset and additional clinical sites: ABIDE GU/KKI/NYU/USM; ADHD200 KKI/NYU; CNP; SRPBS CIN/COI/KTT/KUT/HKH/HRC/HUH/SWA/UTO; Delta AmsterdamUMC; HCP-EP BWH/IU/McL/MGH; KCL; UMich_CWS/SAD/SZG; TOP University of Oslo)

diseases_studied.answer: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD); Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD); Early Psychosis (EP); Schizophrenia (SZ); Bipolar Disorder (BD); Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)

clinical_groups_age.answer: ADHD: 47.6 years, 12.4 SD; ASD: 19.4 years, 11.4 SD; EP: age not fully reported in main demographics; SZ: 31.9 years, 9.5 SD; BD: age not fully reported in main demographics; MDD: 40.1 years, age SD not fully reported in main demographics

clinical_groups_sex.answer: ADHD: F36% M64%; ASD: F14% M86%; EP: sex distribution not fully reported; SZ: F41% M59%; BD: sex distribution not fully reported; MDD: F60% M40%

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score calculated as: Z = (y_observed - y_predicted) / sqrt(σ²_data + σ²_model), where σ²_data is estimated noise variance and σ²_model is variance attributed to modeling uncertainty. Extreme deviations defined as |Z| > 2.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: For each clinical group, individual deviations were summarized by computing the proportion of subjects with extreme deviations (Z>2 for positive, Z<-2 for negative) at each ROI, compared to matched controls from the same sites. Classical case-control comparisons performed using mass-univariate t-tests on both raw cortical thickness/subcortical volumes and on deviation maps, thresholded at Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate p<0.05. Direct contrast of each patient group to their matched controls to avoid nuisance variation confounding effects.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Normative models explained up to 80% of variance out-of-sample across cortex and subcortex, revealed widespread individual variability in clinical cohorts with disorder-specific patterns, and z-statistics from normative deviations provided stronger case-control effects than raw data for most diagnostic groups.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The normative models achieved high out-of-sample performance, explaining up to 80% of variance across cortical and subcortical regions, with similar performance observed in both the full test set (automated QC) and manually quality-checked subset. The models successfully captured known patterns of brain development and aging across different brain regions. When applied to the transdiagnostic psychiatric sample (N=1,985), the models revealed considerable individual variability and heterogeneity among trajectories, with clinical variation being widespread in a fine-grained manner - not all individuals deviated in the same regions and not all disorders had the same characteristic patterns. For most diagnostic groups, z-statistics derived from normative deviations provided stronger case-control effects than analysis of raw cortical thickness data, demonstrating the importance of accurate modeling of population variance. The individual-level deviations provided complementary information to group effects. The transfer validation demonstrated successful generalization to new sites (N=546 from 6 OpenNeuro sites), and the provided software tools enable researchers to adapt the pretrained models to their own datasets.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: The term 'normative' is problematic as it implies normal and abnormal brains; unavoidable sampling bias from aggregating existing data; race, education, and socioeconomic variables not fully available for all datasets with likely WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) sampling bias; UK Biobank contributes 59% of full sample with its own sampling bias; semi-automated QC for full sample does not guarantee complete exclusion of low-quality data; FreeSurfer not adjusted for very young age ranges (2-7 years old) requiring caution when interpreting model in this age range; models are only first step and will need augmentation with more diverse data, different features, and modeling advances.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The authors provide extensive resources for community use including: pretrained models and code for transferring to new sites on GitHub and Zenodo; tutorial code notebooks with sample data that can be run locally or online in web browser via Google Colab; interactive online visualization tool (https://brainvizapp.herokuapp.com/) for exploring evaluation metrics across test sets; transfer demonstration using OpenNeuro datasets showing how to adapt models to new sites not in training set. The authors emphasize the phrase 'reference cohort' should be preferred over 'normative model' and encourage downstream analyses to consider whether the reference cohort is appropriate for the target sample.

general_notes.general_notes: This is a landmark study establishing high-resolution (188 brain regions) lifespan normative models for cortical thickness and subcortical volumes, trained on one of the largest neuroimaging datasets assembled (58,836 individuals from 82 sites). The study represents a major advance over prior work by Bethlehem et al. (2021) which only modeled 4 global measures. Key technical innovations include: (1) use of warped Bayesian linear regression to handle non-Gaussian distributions, (2) B-spline basis expansion for non-linear age effects, (3) comprehensive multi-level validation including held-out test set, manual QC subset, random resampling, transfer to new sites, and clinical application. The full list of 82 sites is documented in Supplementary files 1-2. UK Biobank data processed by UK Biobank team (not by authors), all other sites processed with FreeSurfer v6.0 by the authors. Only first visit included for longitudinal studies (ABCD, UK Biobank). The models are freely available and represent a common reference platform for the field. Site stratification in train-test split is emphasized as critical for addressing MRI scanner confounds. The clinical validation demonstrates both the heterogeneity within disorders and the added value of normative modeling beyond traditional case-control approaches. The paper strongly emphasizes open science with all models, code, documentation, and sample data publicly shared.
